Check whether you have multiple default_action blocks; Terraform compares them as an ordered list, so the API's order wins. Declaring them in the same order the API returns, sorted by their order attribute, normally stops the churn. Some people just add lifecycle { ignore_changes = [default_action] } and move on.

messages.text: need help writing a firm but polite reply to my ex-landlord. he's keeping RM 1,800 of my deposit for 'repainting' and a sofa stain

Happy to help. A few things make a reply like this much stronger: what your tenancy agreement says about deductions, whether you have photos or an inventory from when you moved in, and whether he's given you receipts or quotes. Do you have any of those?
agreement says tenant pays for damage 'beyond fair wear and tear'. I have check-in photos from March 2025 showing the scuffs were already there

That's a good position. Scuffs that pre-date your tenancy can't be charged to you, and ordinary marks on furniture after two years are usually fair wear and tear. The reply should stay calm, cite the clause, refer to the dated photos, and ask for the full deposit back by a specific date.
ok. also unrelated but is there a quick way to get my new address on everything? moved to Mont Kiara last weekend, still figuring out the post

A rough order that works: your bank and card providers first, then LHDN for tax, your employer's HR, insurance, JPJ if you have a car, and any subscriptions. Pos Malaysia also offers mail redirection for a few months, which catches whatever you forget.
lol JPJ, I don't even have a car anymore. sold it in jan
Then skip JPJ, that's one less form. Banks and LHDN are the ones that matter most for official letters.
back to the landlord. if he doesn't budge, what are my options?

You have a few. You could get a lawyer to send a letter of demand, which often settles things quickly. You can also file a claim yourself under the small claims procedure at the Magistrates' Court, which covers amounts up to RM 5,000 and doesn't require a lawyer. Mediation is a third route if both sides are willing.
I'll give him till the 15th. if nothing by then I'm filing at small claims myself, not paying a lawyer for 1,800

That's a sensible plan. Putting the date in your email makes it clear you're serious without sounding aggressive. Keep copies of the agreement, the photos and every message, since you'll need them for the claim form.
put it in the draft. and sign it Kavya Menon, not just Kavya, he's very formal

Here's the draft:

"Dear Mr Marsh,

Thank you for your email. Under clause 7 of our tenancy agreement, deductions apply only to damage beyond fair wear and tear. The wall marks are visible in the check-in photos I sent you in March 2025, and the sofa shows ordinary use. I therefore ask that the full deposit of RM 3,600 be returned. If it is not returned by 15 March 2027, I will file a claim under the small claims procedure at the Magistrates' Court.

Yours sincerely,
Kavya Menon"

messages.text: playwright test flaky: login test passes locally, fails ~30% in CI with 'element is not visible' on the Continue button

Intermittent visibility failures in CI usually mean the test acts before the element has settled. Common causes: animations, a loading overlay still covering the button, or CI being slower so a hard-coded wait is too short. Are you using locators like getByRole, and what does the CI environment look like?
already using getByRole. CI is headless chromium in docker. the button slides in from the bottom, 300ms

That animation is the likely culprit. During the slide-in the button can be outside the viewport or partly covered, so the click races it. Use await expect(button).toBeVisible() before clicking, and consider setting reducedMotion: 'reduce' in the CI config so the app skips the animation entirely. Also check for overlays with the trace viewer.
reducedMotion + toBeVisible fixed it, 50 runs green 🙌
Nice result. It's worth adding reducedMotion to the shared Playwright config so other tests with animations benefit, and keeping trace: 'on-first-retry' so the next flaky failure comes with evidence.

messages.text: explain the difference between a standby letter of credit and a bank guarantee, simply. a client keeps mixing them up

Both protect a beneficiary if the client fails to perform. A bank guarantee is the bank directly promising to pay if the client defaults, and it's governed by local law or the URDG rules. A standby letter of credit is technically a letter of credit used as a backup, governed by ISP98 or UCP600, and is more common in US-linked deals. In practice: same purpose, different paperwork and rules.
nice, one line version?
"Both are the bank's promise to pay if you don't; a guarantee is the classic local form, an SBLC is the international, letter-of-credit form of the same idea."
